source_text: Unum igitur gradum insistimus, et in hoc solum provocamus, an praecepta sint a Deo martyria, ut credas ratione praecepta, si praecepta cognoveris, quia nihil Deus non ratione praeceperit. Siquidem honorata est apud illum mors religiosorum ipsius, ut canit David; non opinor ista communis et omnium debitum: atqui justa, etiam ignominiosa est ex elogio transgressionis et merito damnationis; sed illa quae in ipso aditur ex testimonio religionis, et praelio confessionis, pro justitia et sacramento; sicut Esaia: Videte, inquit, quomodo perit justus, et nemo excipit corde; et viri justi auferuntur, et nemo animadvertit: a facie enim injustitiae perit justus, et erit honor sepultura ejus. Habes hic quoque et praedicationem et remunerationem martyriorum. A primordio enim justitia vim patitur. Statim ut coli Deus coepit, invidiam religio sortita est: qui Deo placuerat, occiditur, et quidem a fratre; quo proclivius impietas alienum sanguinem sectaretur, a suo auspicata est. Denique, non modo justorum; verum etiam et prophetarum. David exagitatur, Elias fugatur, Jeremias lapidatur, Esaias secatur, Zacharias inter altare et aedem trucidatur, perennes cruoris sui maculas silicibus adsignans. Ipse clausula Legis et Prophetarum; nec prophetes, sed angelus dictus, contumeliosa caede truncatur in puellae psalticae lucar. Et utique qui spiritu Dei agebantur, ab ipso in martyria dirigebantur, ut et jam patiendo quae et praedicassent. Proinde et trina fraternitas, cum dedicatio imaginis regiae urbem urgeret officio, non ignoraverunt quid fides, quae sola in illis captiva non fuerat, exigeret; moriendum scilicet adversus idololatriam. Meminerant enim et Jeremiae scribentis ad eos, quibus illa captivitas imminebat: Et nunc videbitis deos Babyloniorum aureos et argenteos et ligneos portari super humeros, ostentantes nationibus timorem. Cavete igitur ne et vos consimiles sitis Allophylis, et timore capiamini, dum aspicitis turbas adorantes retro eos et ante; sed dicite in animo vestro: Te, Domine, adorare debemus. Itaque dixerunt a Deo concepta fiducia, quando vigore animi conditionales minas regis excutiunt: Non habemus necessitatem respondendi huic tuo imperio. Est enim Deus noster quem colimus, potens eruere nos de fornace ignis, et ex manibus tuis; et tunc manifestum fiet tibi, quod neque idolo tuo famulabimur, nec imaginem tuam auream, quam stauisti, adorabimus. O martyrium et sine passione perfectum! Satis passi, satis exusti sunt, quos propterea Deus texit, ne potestatem ejus mentiri viderentur. Nam et Danielem nullius praeter Dei supplicem, et idcirco a Chaldaeis delatum ac depostulatum, statim utique conclusa et usitata feritas leonum devorasset, si Darii digna praesumptio de Deo falli debuisset. Caeterum, pati oportebat omnem Dei praedicatorem atque cultorem qui ad idololatriam provocatus negasset obsequium, secundum illius quoque rationis statum, qua et praesentibus tunc et posteris deinceps commendari veritatem oportebat, pro qua fidem diceret passio ipsorum defensorum ejus; quia nemo voluisset occidi, nisi compos veritatis. Talia a primordio et praecepta et exempla debitricem martyrii fidem ostendunt.
thought_title: Martyrdom as a Requirement of Faith
pass_a_gloss: Therefore we insist on one step, and in this alone we challenge, whether martyrdoms are commandments from God, so that you may believe the commandments by reason, if you have recognized the commandments, because God has not commanded anything without reason. For indeed death of the religious is honored with Him, as David sings; I do not think that this is a common debt of all, but rather a just one, and even an ignominious one due to the transgression and the merit of condemnation; but that which is added to it from the testimony of religion and the battle of confession, for justice and for a sacrament; just as Isaiah says: Behold, how the just man perishes, and no one takes it to heart; and just men are taken away, and no one notices: for the just man perishes from the face of injustice, and his burial will be honorable. You have here also the preaching and the reward of martyrs. For from the beginning justice suffers violence. As soon as God began to be worshiped, religion incurred envy; he who had pleased God was killed, and indeed by his brother; whence impiety more readily pursued the blood of strangers, having been begun from its own. Finally, not only of the just, but also of the prophets. David is troubled, Elijah is fleeing, Jeremiah is stoned, Isaiah is sawn, Zachariah is slaughtered between the altar and the temple, assigning perpetual stains of his blood to the stones. He himself, the conclusion of the Law and the Prophets, not a prophet, but an angel, is killed with a contemptuous slaughter in the grove of a psalm-singing girl. And certainly those who were led by the Spirit of God were directed by Him into martyrdoms, so that they might also suffer what they had preached. Therefore, the three brothers, when the dedication of the royal image was pressing the city with its duty, did not ignore what faith, which alone was not captive in them, demanded; namely, to die against idolatry. For they remembered Jeremiah writing to them, to whom that captivity was looming: And now you will see the golden and silver and wooden gods of the Babylonians being carried on shoulders, showing fear to the nations. Beware, therefore, lest you also become like the foreigners, and be taken by fear, while you see the crowds worshiping behind them and before; but say in your heart: We ought to adore You, Lord. And so they spoke, having conceived confidence from God, when they shook off the conditional threats of the king with the strength of their spirit: We have no need to respond to your command. For our God, whom we worship, is able to rescue us from the fiery furnace and from your hands; and then it will be clear to you that we will neither serve your idol nor worship the golden image that you have set up. Oh, martyrdom perfected even without suffering! They have suffered enough, they have been burned enough, those whom God protected, lest they seem to deny His power. For also Daniel, a suppliant of God alone, and for that reason accused and demanded by the Chaldeans, would have been devoured at once by the usual ferocity of the lions, if the worthy presumption of Darius about God had to fail. Moreover, it was necessary for every preacher and worshiper of God, who had been provoked to idolatry and had denied obedience, to suffer, according to the state of that reason also, by which the truth had to be commended to those present then and to posterity, for which they would say their passion was a defense; because no one would have wanted to be killed, unless he was in possession of the truth. Such things from the beginning, both commandments and examples, show that faith is indebted to martyrdom.

bible_refs.note: Behold, how the just man perishes

pass_b_english: We press a single point, and this alone is our challenge: are martyrdoms divine commands? Recognize that, and you will trust the commands by reason, because God never commands anything without reason. After all, the death of His faithful ones is honored in His sight, as David sings (Psalm 116:15). I do not take this for the common debt owed by all; that death is just, yes, but ignominious, the wages of transgression and deserved condemnation. The death that is added to it, though — the death born of religious witness and the battle of confession, for justice and for a sacrament — that is another matter. As Isaiah says: "See how the righteous perishes, and no one takes it to heart; the devout are taken away, and no one understands. From the face of injustice the righteous perishes, and his burial will be in peace" (Isaiah 57:1-2). Here you have both the preaching and the reward of martyrs.

From the very beginning, justice has suffered violence. The moment God began to be worshiped, religion drew envy's aim: the man who pleased God was murdered, and by his own brother at that — so that impiety, having tasted blood at home, would more readily hunt the blood of strangers. In the end, not only the just but the prophets as well. David was hounded, Elijah driven into flight, Jeremiah stoned, Isaiah sawn in two, Zachariah slaughtered between altar and sanctuary, stamping the stones with perpetual stains of his blood (Jeremiah). The very climax of the Law and the Prophets — not a prophet but an angel — was cut down by a contemptuous slaughter for the fee of a psalm-singing girl. And certainly those who were driven by the Spirit of God were directed by Him into martyrdoms, so that they might also suffer what they had preached.

So too the three brothers. When the dedication of the royal image pressed the city with its duty, they did not ignore what faith — which alone had not been taken captive in them — demanded: to die rather than serve idolatry. They remembered Jeremiah writing to them as that captivity loomed: "And now you will see the golden, silver, and wooden gods of the Babylonians carried on shoulders, striking fear into the nations. Take care, therefore, that you do not become like the foreigners, and be seized with fear when you see the crowds worshiping before and behind them; but say in your hearts: 'You, Lord, we must worship'" (Jeremiah). And so they spoke, their confidence conceived from God, when they shook off the king's conditional threats with the strength of their spirit: "We have no need to answer you on this. The God we worship is able to deliver us from the fiery furnace and from your hand; and then it will be clear to you that we will neither serve your god nor worship the golden image you have set up" (Daniel 3:16-18). Oh, a martyrdom perfected without suffering! They suffered enough, they were scorched enough — those whom God shielded, lest His power seem a lie.

Nor was Daniel spared the pattern. A suppliant of God alone, he was denounced and demanded by the Chaldeans; the lions' accustomed ferocity would have devoured him at once, had Darius's worthy confidence in God been allowed to fail. Moreover, it was necessary for every preacher and worshiper of God who, provoked to idolatry, refused obedience, to suffer — in keeping with that same logic by which the truth had to be commended to those present then and to posterity afterward, for which their passion would stand as the truth's defense; because no one would choose to be killed unless he possessed the truth. Such things from the beginning — both commandments and examples — prove that faith is indebted to martyrdom.

review.notes: All clauses in the Latin source were checked against Pass A and Pass B. Scripture citations (Isaiah 57:1-2, Jeremiah, Daniel 3:16-18, Psalm 116:15) were correctly identified and added to the English text as required. Pass A preserves the sense of all clauses, and Pass B provides a fluent rendering that does not contradict the Latin or Pass A. The title 'Martyrdom as a Requirement of Faith' accurately reflects the thought of the text.
